title: How to price your paperback without guessing
summary: A simple way to set a price that covers printing, pays you something real and still looks normal next to similar books.

body.p: Your price has to do three things: cover the printing cost, leave you money for each copy, and look normal next to books like yours. Get any one wrong and sales or profit suffer.
Every printer has a calculator on its website. Put in your page count, trim size, paper and ink (black or color). Write the number down in your book's business tracker in the Author Studio.

body.h: Step 2: Look at 10 books like yours

body.p: Search your genre and page length. Write down 10 paperback prices from books that look and feel like yours. Most will sit in a narrow band. That band is your target.

Each store keeps a share of the price and takes out the printing cost. Use the store's own royalty calculator with your price and page count. If you'd keep less than you're comfortable with, try the top of the band, or look at a smaller trim size or fewer pages.
Prices like $14.99 or $16.99 look familiar to shoppers. An odd price can make a book look off, even if nobody can say why.
Color printing costs much more per page. Many children's book authors keep the page count low, use a smaller size, or offer a paperback and a hardcover at two prices so families can choose.

body.tip: Write down every cost you pay for this book (editing, cover, ISBN, proof copies, ads) in the Author Studio tracker. Knowing your real costs is how you know when the book has paid for itself.
